translations.text: A homily for Holy Thursday by John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.
On Judas’s betrayal, on [?], and on the explanation of the holy mysteries.
And on not bearing grudges. Today it is necessary to speak briefly to you, my beloved. It is necessary to speak briefly,
not because you find the abundance of what is said burdensome. For no other city can be found
so lovingly devoted to listening to spiritual words.
Rather, today there is a compelling reason for brevity. For I see many of the faithful
going to partake of the awe-inspiring mysteries. So that they may neither miss that table nor be deprived of it,
we must prepare a meal today, so that perhaps you may benefit from both.
Having had your fill of this table and of our words, you may then depart, and with fear and trembling
and fitting self-restraint approach the awe-inspiring and fearful Communion.
For today, beloved, our Lord Jesus was betrayed. Rather, grieve and weep bitterly,
not for Jesus, who was betrayed, but for Judas, who betrayed him.
For Jesus, who was betrayed, saved the whole world, but Judas, who betrayed him, destroyed his own soul.
The one who was betrayed sits at the Father’s right hand in heaven, but the one who betrayed him is now in Hades. Eternal
torment is what he awaits. Groan for him; weep for him, since our Lord himself wept for him.
For when he saw him, he was troubled and said, declaring, “One of you will betray me.” Why was he sorrowful?
He also showed his love, teaching us that it is not the one who suffers wrong, but the one who does wrong
whom we should always mourn. For this is worse than the other. Rather, suffering wrong is not an evil, but doing wrong is an evil.
For suffering wrong gains us the kingdom of heaven, but doing wrong
makes us liable to eternal fire and torment. For he said, “Blessed are those chosen for righteousness’ sake,
for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Do you see that suffering wrong
has as its reward and gift the kingdom of heaven? Hear how doing wrong brings torment and suffering.
For after Paul said of the Jews that they killed the Lord and drove out the prophets, he added, “Their end
will be according to their deeds.” Do you see how those whom they persecute receive the kingdom,
while the persecutors receive wrath? I have not said these things now without a reason.
But let us not be angry with our enemies; instead, let us have mercy on them, weep for them, and care for them.
For those who are hostile toward us are suffering terribly. If we put our souls in this condition, we can also pray for them.

For this reason, this is now the fourth day that I have been speaking with you about prayer for enemies, so that the message of this teaching may become firmly established through frequent instruction,
being received. For this reason, we wash ourselves frequently with words, so that we might soothe and stop the irritation of anger.
Let whoever approaches prayer be free from anger. For Christ teaches this not only for the sake of our enemies,
but also for our sake, as we forgive their sins. You will receive more than this if you give.
You forgive your enemy a sin. “Then how will I receive more?” someone says. You forgive your enemy’s sins, and you will be forgiven for what you have sinned against the Master.
Those sins are without healing and without mercy, but these have much consolation and mercy.
Listen, then, to Eli speaking to his sons, if they sinned:
“If a person sins against another person, someone prays for him. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”
Even prayer will not easily soften that wound. Prayer will not soften it,
but forgiveness of an enemy’s sins will soften it. Therefore God called those sins ten thousand talents,
the sins against the Master, but these a hundred denarii. Forgive a hundred denarii, so that you may be forgiven ten thousand talents.
Now that we have spoken enough about prayer, let us return again to the subject of the betrayal.
Let us see how our Master was betrayed. “Then one of the twelve went,
the one called Judas Iscariot, to the chief priests:
‘What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?’” I think that what is being said is clear,
and that there is nothing further to [?]. But if someone carefully examines each
of the things reported, it has many aspects and a great depth of meaning. First, the time:
for the evangelist did not indicate it without a reason. He did not simply say, “He went,” but added, “Then he went.” Then—
when? Tell me. And why does he indicate the time? What does he want you to learn? “Then” was not said to you without a reason.
He speaks by the Spirit. And whoever speaks by the Spirit says nothing without a reason or without meaning. What, then, does “then” mean?
Before that time, before that hour, a prostitute came carrying a flask of fragrant ointment
and poured that olive oil onto the Lord’s head. She showed great faith.
She showed great healing, great obedience and self-restraint. She withdrew from temporal life.
He became better and wiser. And when the prostitute repented, when she recognized the Master,
then the disciple betrayed the Teacher. For this reason he said, “Then,” so that you would not accuse the Teacher of weakness
when you see the disciple betraying him. For so great was the Teacher’s power
that he could draw even a prostitute to obey him. What, then? Could he who drew the prostitute
not draw the disciple? He could have drawn the disciple too, but he did not wish to make him good by force
or draw him to himself by compulsion. “Then he went.” This expression, “he went,” also has considerable significance.
For he was not summoned by the chief priests, he says, nor was he compelled, but without compulsion, on his own,
at home he conceived an evil scheme and devised a plan for himself, without a single adviser
or friend. “Then one of the twelve went.” What does “one of the twelve” mean?
This too shows his great [?], in saying, “one of the twelve.”
For Jesus had other disciples as well, seventy in number.
But those were of the second rank. They did not have so great an honor or such freedom of access.
They did not share in such great mysteries. The twelve were chosen above these,
and these were [?]. These were the company around the Teacher, and Judas broke away from them.
But so that you might learn that it was not an ordinary disciple who betrayed him, but one of the chosen company,
he therefore said, “one of the twelve.” And Matthew is not ashamed to write this.
Why is he not ashamed? So that you might learn that everywhere they tell the whole truth
and conceal nothing, even when it is thought disgraceful.
For this very thing that seems disgraceful reveals the Master’s love for humanity: that a traitor, a robber, a thief
he deemed worthy of so much good, and continued to bear with him even until the Last Supper.
For he instructed him and taught him and cared for him in every way. Therefore, do not despair of yourself
when you look at the prostitute. Nor, again, be confident in yourself when you look at Judas.
For both are destructive: self-confidence and despair. Self-confidence causes the one who stands to fall,
while despair does not allow the one who lies fallen to rise. For this reason Paul teaches, saying,
“Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall.” You have examples of both.
How the disciple who thought he stood fell! How the prostitute who lay fallen rose! Our mind is slippery.
Our thinking is unstable. For this reason, we must strengthen and guard ourselves on every side.
Then one of the Twelve, Judas Iscariot, went away. Do you see from what a position he fell?
Do you see how much teaching he disregarded? Do you see what a great evil laziness and growing cold are?
Judas, called Iscariot. Why do you tell me his town?
I wish I had not even known him! Judas, known as Iscariot. Why, then,
does he tell us his town? There was another disciple named Judas, called the Zealot.
So that their having the same name should cause no confusion, he distinguished this one from the other.
He identified the other by his virtue: Judas the Zealot. But he did not identify this one by his wickedness, for he did not say, “Judas the betrayer.”
Yet it would have been fitting, just as he named the other by his virtue, to name this one by his wickedness and say,
“Judas the betrayer.” But to teach you to keep your tongue free of slander,
he holds back even in speaking of the betrayer himself. Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went
to the chief priests and said to them, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?”
Oh, those loathsome words! How did they burst from his mouth? How did he move his tongue? How did his whole body not
go numb? How did he not lose his mind? “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?”
Tell me, was this what the Teacher taught you? Was it not for this reason that he said, “Do not acquire gold or silver
or copper in your belts”? On the mountain he had already warned you [?] in his teaching about the love of money.
Was this not what he always taught? And afterward he said, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek,
turn the other to him also.” “What are you willing to give me?” What madness! “And I will hand him over to you.”
Tell me, why? What fault, small or great, can you find with him, that you betray the Teacher? Is it because he gave you
authority over demons? Because he enabled you to cure diseases? Because he enabled you to cleanse lepers? Because he enabled you to raise the dead?
Because he set you above the power of death? Is this the repayment you give for these benefits?
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” Oh, madness—or rather, oh, love of money!
For it produced all this evil. With his mind fixed on it, this man betrayed the Teacher. For such is that evil root:
fiercer than a demon. It [?] the souls it has ensnared and makes them forget everything.
both himself and his neighbors, and the laws of nature. It will drive even him out and make him foolish.
For see how much it then drove out of Judas’s soul: conversation, familiar companionship,
fellowship at the table, miracles, teaching, admonition, instruction—all these
the love of money then consigned to oblivion. So Paul, too, rightly said
that the love of money is the root of all evil.
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” What great madness there is in these words!
Tell me, are you handing over the one who holds all things together, who rules over demons, who rebukes the sea,
the Master of all creation? But to restrain his madness and teach him
that if he had not been [?], he would not have given himself up, listen to what he does at the moment when he gives himself up.
When they came against him with clubs and torches, he said to them, “Whom are you looking for?”
And they did not recognize the one they wanted to arrest. So far was Judas from being able to hand him over
that he did not even see the one standing there whom he wanted to hand over, although there were torches and so much light.
For the evangelist emphasized this when he said, “They had torches, and it was light, yet they did not see him.”
For he continually reminded him each day, showing by deeds and words that the betrayer would not escape.
Yet he did not openly expose him before everyone, lest he make him more shameless.
Nor did he remain silent, lest Judas, thinking he could escape unnoticed, begin to betray him without fear.
He often said, “One of you will betray me,” but he did not openly identify him.
He also spoke many words about the Day of Judgment, and many about the kingdom of heaven.
He showed his power in both respects: to punish those who had sinned and to honor those who had walked the right path.
But he disregarded all this, and God did not compel him by force. For he gave us control over both evil and good deeds,
since he wants us to be good willingly. Therefore, if we are unwilling, he does not compel us, for being forced to be good is not good.
For he, too, was master of his own mind, and of his own will he refused to obey,
but turned to the love of money. Because of this he became blind in his mind and betrayed his Savior, saying:
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” Thus, exposing his madness, the evangelist said:
“When they arrived, Judas was standing near them”—the very one who had said:
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” It is not from this alone that one can see Christ’s power.
But when he had uttered a brief word, they went away. Yet since even then they would not abandon their shameful conduct,
he willingly hands himself over, all but saying, “I have done everything on my part.
I have revealed my power and shown that the deeds you are attempting are powerless. I wanted to put an end to your wickedness.
But since you are unwilling and still persist in your wickedness, here I am, handing myself over.”
I have told you this so that no one may slander Christ by saying, “Why did he not turn Judas toward good?
Why did he not make him wise and gentle?” But how was he to make Judas gentle? By force or by free choice?
If by force, he did not wish to become better even in this way. No one becomes good by compulsion.
But if by free choice, everything can be put right. He was given free choice. So if he did not wish to accept medicinal herbs to help him,
the fault is not the physician’s, but belongs to the one who did not want healing. Consider how much he did to turn him back,
to save him from that. He taught him all wisdom, both through deeds and through words.
He made him greater than demons and gave him the power to perform many miracles. He frightened him with the fire to come.
He sought to win him over with the promise of the kingdom. He often exposed his thoughts.
Yet even as he exposed him, he did not identify him openly. He washed his feet along with the others’.
He also gave him a share at the table. He lacked nothing, small or great. Yet he willingly persisted in his own destruction.
And so that you may learn that, although he was able to change, he did not wish to, but that everything happened to him through his own negligence:
after betraying him, he threw down the thirty denarii. And what did he say? “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.”
What happened when he saw him performing miracles? He did not say, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,”
but, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” For when evil had taken hold and the betrayal was at its end,
and the sin had been completed, then he recognized his sin. What, then, do I learn from this? That when we are [?], no
instruction will benefit us. But when we make an effort, we also stir ourselves toward good.
For when his teacher instructed him, he did not listen. But when no one was instructing him, he then became aware of his own conscience,
and with no teacher present, he changed. Repenting of his brazen deeds, he threw down the thirty pieces of silver.
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” And they set thirty pieces of silver for him. They set a price on blood beyond price.
Why do you take thirty pieces of silver, Judas? Christ came freely.
to shed his blood for the whole world—the blood over which you bargain and make a deal, shameless man.
For what could be more shameless than this bargain? Then the disciples came. Then—when?
When this happened, when the betrayal took hold, when Judas destroyed himself.
His disciples came to him, saying to him, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
Look at the disciples; look at the disciple. He betrays the Master, while they concern themselves with serving him. He makes a plot,
while they prepare to serve. Both they and he shared in the same things: the same miracles, the same teachings,
the same instruction. Where, then, did the difference come from? From their will: that is the whole cause,
everywhere, for both good and evil people. “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
Christ’s. It was evening then. Since the Master had no home,
they therefore say, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” I have no fixed lodging,
I have neither a shelter nor a house. Let those who build splendid houses and spacious porticoes
and long courtyards learn that Christ had nowhere to lay his head. That is why they ask,
“Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” Which Passover? Not this Passover, but the Jewish one.
The disciples prepared that one, but he himself established this Passover of ours. Indeed, he himself became the Passover.
“Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” That was the Jewish Passover; it had its beginning in Egypt.
Why, then, does Christ eat that Passover? Because he fulfilled everything prescribed by the Law.
For when he was baptized, he said, “For it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.”
“I have come,” he said, “to redeem humanity from the lawless curse.” For God sent his own Son,
born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those under the Law
and bring the Law itself to an end. But so that no one might say that he abolished the Law for this reason,
that he put an end to it because he could not fulfill it, as though it were burdensome,
he first fulfilled all its requirements and then set it aside. That is why he also celebrated the Passover. For the Passover was
a commandment of the Law. And why did the Law command them to eat the Passover? The Jews were unmindful of their benefactor,
and immediately forgot the good deeds of God their protector. For [?] when they came out of Egypt,
having seen the sea part and close again, and many other miracles, they said, “Make gods for us.”
who will go before us. What are you saying, while holding miracles in your hand? And yet have you so soon forgotten God, your benefactor?
Since they were so unfeeling and ignorant, God tied the remembrance of his gifts to the festivals.
For this reason he commanded them to sacrifice the Passover lamb. “If your son asks you,” he said, “what this Passover means,”
you shall say this: “The children smeared the doors with sheep’s blood in Egypt.
Then the destroyer came, and when he saw it, he did not dare rush in and bring the plague upon you.”
And the festival was a perpetual remembrance of their deliverance. Moreover, they had not only this,
which reminded them of the benefits they had received in the past, but also something else, something greater,
which showed them beforehand what was to come. For that lamb was only a figure
of another, spiritual Lamb. Both were sheep, but one was a shadow and the other the reality.
But when the Sun of Righteousness appeared, the shadow ceased. When the sun rises, the shadow disappears.
For this reason both Passovers took place at that table: the figurative one and the true one.
For just as painters sketch figures on a single panel and paint the reality in color,
so Christ also did at that table: he sketched the figurative Passover
and added the true one. “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” This was the Jewish Passover.
But when the sun has come, let the light no longer shine. When the reality has come, the shadow is useless.
I say these things to the Jews, since they think they are celebrating Passover, since with a shameful mind
they set out unleavened bread, though they are always uncircumcised in heart.
Tell me, Jew, how do you celebrate Passover? The temple has been torn down, the altars demolished, the Holy of Holies shut.
Every sacrificial offering has ceased. Why do you dare to engage in these unlawful deeds?
You once went to Babylon, and there those who had taken you captive said, “Sing us a song of the Lord,” and you could not.
And David, showing this, said: “By the river of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.
On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments,” that is, harps, pipes,
flutes, and the rest. For the old order used these, and they sang songs with them.
And when they went into captivity, they took these with them, so that they might have a reminder of life
in their own land, but not so that they might sing. “For there,” he said, “those who had taken us captive asked us for the words of songs. We said:
How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?
What are you saying? You will not sing the Lord’s songs in a foreign land, yet you celebrate the Lord’s Passover in a foreign land?
Do you see the foolishness? Do you see the lawlessness? When there were enemies compelling them,
they could not even sing a song in a foreign land. But now, of their own accord, with no one compelling them
or afflicting them, they wage war against God. Do you see how impious the use of unleavened bread is?
How lawless the festival is? How the Passover is no longer Jewish? There was once a Jewish Passover, but now it has been abolished,
and the spiritual Passover has come, which he handed down then. For while they were eating and drinking, he spoke to them.
Taking bread, he broke it and said, “This is my flesh, broken for you.”
Those who have been instructed understand what is being said. And again, taking the cup, he said, “This is my blood,
which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” And Judas came while Christ was saying this.
This is the blood, Judas, which you sold for thirty denarii.
This is the blood for whose sake you so often held those shameful consultations
with the foolish Pharisees. How great is Christ’s love for humanity! How great is Judas’s lawlessness!
How great his madness! For he sold it for thirty denarii,
yet even after this Christ did not refuse to give this blood that had been sold for the forgiveness of sins, if only he had been willing. For
Judas came to partake of the holy table. Just as he washed his feet when he washed those of the other disciples,
so he also gave him the holy offerings, so that he would have no excuse at all if he persisted in evil.
For Christ did everything that was his to do, but Judas nevertheless persisted in his evil purpose.
But now it is time to approach this glorious table. Let us all come,
then, with fitting self-restraint and purity. Let no one here be a Judas. Let no one be evil.
Let no one harbor poison. Let no one have one thing in his mouth and another in his mind.
Christ has come, and he is the same now. He who prepared that table also prepares this one now.
For it is not a human being who makes the offerings set before us become Christ’s flesh and blood, but Christ, who was crucified for us.
The priest performs the outward rite, speaking those words, but the power and grace are entirely God’s.
“This is my flesh,” he said. This word transforms the offerings set before us.
And just as that voice says, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.”
It was spoken once, but its effect continues through all ages, giving our nature the power to bear offspring.
So too this voice, spoken once, continually, at the table in the churches, from that time until today
and until his coming, makes the sacrifice complete. Therefore let no one approach with deceit.
Let no one be [?] with malice. Let no one have poison
in his mind, lest he receive condemnation. For at that time, when Judas took the bread,
the devil immediately leaped into him, not despising the Lord’s body, but despising Judas’s shamelessness.
Learn from this that those who receive Holy Communion unworthily
are all the more often assailed and entered by the devil, just as Judas was then. For these things flow in purity to the worthy,
but bring those who receive them unworthily into greater punishment. I say this not to frighten you,
but rather to strengthen you. Let no one here be a Judas, harboring the poison of evil. The sacrifice is spiritual food.
Just as bodily food, when it enters a stomach containing harmful mucus, prolongs the illness,
not because of its own nature but because of the stomach’s sickness, so it is with the spiritual mysteries.
For when these enter a mind full of malice, they drive it still further away and destroy it,
not because of their own nature, but because of the sickness of the soul that receives them. Therefore let no one harbor an evil mind within himself.
Instead, let us cleanse our hearts, for we are approaching a pure sacrifice. Let us make our souls holy.
For this can happen in a single day. How, and in what way? If you have anything against your enemy,
uproot your anger, heal the wound, put an end to your hostility, so that you may receive healing from the table.
You are approaching a majestic and holy sacrifice. Stand in awe of the meaning of that offering. Slain,
Christ lies before you. For this reason he was slain—and why? To reconcile the things of heaven, and to make you a friend of the angels.
And Christ reconciles all things to God, so that both with the angels and with the Lord of the angels
he might bring you into friendship, though you were an enemy and an adversary. He gave his own life, yet you hesitate over your fellow servant,
holding on to hostility. How can you approach the Lord’s table of peace?
He did not refuse to die for you, yet you are unwilling even to let go of your anger against your fellow servant.
“But,” someone says, “he did me great harm and utterly wore me down.” What of it? Even if the loss of possessions is severe [?].
But he never crucified you as the Jews crucified Christ. Yet Christ gives even that very blood which they shed
for the salvation of those who shed it. What can you say in answer to this if you do not abandon your hostility toward your enemy?
For you have harmed not him, but rather yourself. You have often harmed him in this life,
but you have also made your own reckoning on Judgment Day merciless. God hates nothing so much
as a person who bears grudges, for this reveals an inflamed heart and a puffed-up soul.
Listen to what he said: “When you bring your gift to the altar and there, standing before the altar, remember
that your brother has something against you, leave your gift and go and be reconciled with your brother.”
What are you saying? Am I to leave it? “Yes,” he said, “for this sacrifice too is for reconciliation with your brother.
Yet you do not establish peace, though you partake of that sacrifice. Your action is therefore senseless.
First, then, do that for which the sacrifice was offered, so that afterward you may eat your fill to good purpose.
For this reason the Son of God came down: to reconcile our nature with God. For this reason he not only came himself,
but also promised that we who do the same would share his name. For he said, “Blessed are the peacemakers,
for they will be called sons of God.” For what the only-begotten Son of God did,
you too will do according to your ability, bringing about peace both for yourself and for us.
For this reason he also calls you a son of God when you make peace. For this reason, at harvest time,
he mentioned no other righteous deed separately, but only being at peace with everyone,
showing that this is greater than everything else. I wanted to prolong my discourse, but [?] the things agreed upon
for the listeners, if they remember. Let us therefore always remember these words, [?] the holy kisses, the approaching kiss
that we exchange with one another. For this binds our minds together and makes us all one body,
since we also partake of one flesh. Let us all, then, unite into one body, not mingling our flesh with one another,
but joining our souls together in a bond of love.
In this way we can eat freely and fully from the table set before us. For even if we have countless righteous deeds, but bear grudges,
all this is senseless and in vain, and none of these things can produce the fruit of the word that leads to salvation.
Knowing this, let us put aside all anger, cleansing our consciences,
and let us approach Christ’s table with gentleness and complete calm.
With him be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
